title: Peter Claver (1580–1654)
hook: in Cartagena he met every slave ship and called himself the slave of the slaves

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martin de Porres, the brother in Lima who swept floors and nursed the city's poor. Your line was the saint with a broom. What humble job did you pick up? Today the story moves north, to the Caribbean. Day eight hundred sixty.

Word comes into the port of Cartagena that a ship has been sighted. For the merchants, that means cargo. For the people in the hold, it means the end of a voyage they were forced to make in chains, sick, starving, some of them dying. And for one Spanish Jesuit, it means he goes down to the docks with baskets of food, water, lemons and medicine, and climbs down into the hold. This is a hard story, and it should be told plainly. Today, Peter Claver.
screen: `A SHIP IS SIGHTED.` → `PEOPLE IN CHAINS IN THE HOLD.` → `A PRIEST CLIMBS DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Cartagena, on the Caribbean coast of what is now Colombia, was a port where enslaved Africans were brought and sold. Claver, a Spanish Jesuit, was sent there as a young man. Before he left Spain, an elderly Jesuit brother, Alphonsus Rodriguez, a doorkeeper, had urged him toward the people no one cared for. Second, the docks. When a ship came in, Claver went aboard and below decks. He brought food and water first, and washed and bandaged the sick. He used interpreters to speak to people in their own languages. He taught and baptized those who asked. He followed them into the yards where they were held, and later visited them on plantations and in hospitals. Third, the vow. When he made his final vows as a Jesuit, he signed his name with a phrase in Latin: the slave of the Africans forever. The saying passed down as slave of the slaves. Fourth, the honest part. Claver did not end the slave trade, and the Church of his day did not condemn it outright. He served inside an evil he could not stop, and those who tell his story now try to remember both: his love, and the system it ran into. Jesus's words in Matthew's Gospel read like the job description he took on, in the Douay-Rheims: "I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink." Near the end of his life Claver was sick and largely forgotten, cared for poorly himself. The Church later named him a saint, and Catholics invoke him as a patron of enslaved people.
screen: `CARTAGENA: A SLAVE PORT.` · `DOWN INTO THE HOLD.` · `SLAVE OF THE AFRICANS FOREVER.` · `HE COULDN'T STOP IT. HE SERVED.` · then, large: `I WAS HUNGRY, AND YOU GAVE ME TO EAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for victims of slavery today, or hold them in mind. Settle, and breathe. Forced labor did not end with the ships. People are still trafficked, held in debt, made to work without pay or freedom, sometimes close to where you live. You don't need names. Let them be present, the way the people in the hold were present to Claver. If you pray, you can ask Peter Claver to pray for them, or pray an Our Father slowly. If you don't, simply stay with them, and let it cost you a little. The bell holds the time.
Peter Claver. A Spanish Jesuit in Cartagena who met the slave ships with food and medicine, and called himself the slave of the Africans forever.
Your line: slave of the slaves. Today, before you buy something, pause for one breath and remember the hands that made it. Day eight hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Peter Claver and invoke him as a patron of enslaved people and of ministry to African-descended communities; some parishes mark it with prayer for victims of human trafficking.

fork.setup: you're Claver. a slave ship has just docked, and the people below are sick and starving. what do you bring down first?
fork.reveal: he brought food, water and medicine first, washed the sick, and only then taught those who asked.

original.note: Latin: 'slave of the Africans forever', the phrase Claver signed with his final vows (aethiops was the old Latin word for an African).

trapdoor: what you thought: a missionary who baptized slaves.
what it means: a Jesuit who met the ships with food and medicine and called himself the slaves' slave.
what a scholar hears: he signed his vows in Latin, aethiopum semper servus, slave of the Africans forever.

notes: Claims rule: the voice avoids dates and counts. The index hook says he met 'every' slave ship; the voice says 'when a ship came in' instead. Confirm.
'Many of them dying' in the hook describes the Middle Passage generally; confirm wording or soften.
Confirm: Alphonsus Rodriguez's encouragement in Majorca; use of interpreters; visits to yards, plantations and hospitals; neglect in his final illness.
Original: 'aethiopum semper servus' and pronunciation in ecclesiastical Latin; confirm the exact phrase of his signature.
'The Church of his day did not condemn it outright' is a sensitive historical claim; confirm the phrasing is fair.
Practice suggests the Our Father (an existing prayer), offered only to those who pray.

Editor pass: the review said the story moved 'north along the coast' from Lima to Cartagena, which are on different oceans; now 'north, to the Caribbean'. Hook 'many of them dying' softened to 'some'; trapdoor 'met every ship' changed to 'met the ships' (no source for every).

Second editor: 'Catholics today remember both' (a sweeping claim) narrowed to those who tell his story; 'the Church named him a patron of the enslaved' now 'Catholics invoke him as a patron', since the formal patronage wording is not in the cited source.
Audit: the original's pronunciation stressed the wrong syllable; Aethiopum has a short penult (Greek Aithiopes), so the stress falls on the antepenult: eh-TEE-oh-poom.
